entry.title: Bain Capital's Special Situations Asia III Reports $1.81bn First Close
entry.summary: Bain Capital's third Asia-focused Special Situations fund has reported $1.81 billion in capital raised, continuing the firm's fundraising activity in the region. Bain Capital Special Situations Asia III, L.P. reported $1.81 billion in total sales in October 2026, representing its first reported fundraising milestone. The fund's offering remains open, with…
entry.content:
Bain Capital's third Asia-focused Special Situations fund has reported $1.81 billion in capital raised, continuing the firm's fundraising activity in the region.

Bain Capital Special Situations Asia III, L.P. reported $1.81 billion in total sales in October 2026, representing its first reported fundraising milestone. The fund's offering remains open, with its final close yet to be established.

Bain Capital's Special Situations strategy provides capital to businesses and asset-backed opportunities through situations requiring financing beyond conventional lending or equity structures. Its investment approach spans corporate and asset-backed credit, structured capital solutions, distressed situations, growth capital, balance-sheet restructuring and business transitions.

The third Asia vehicle follows Bain Capital Special Situations Asia II, L.P., which closed in 2022 with more than $2.06 billion in commitments against a $1.5 billion target.

entry.title: Motive Partners' Venture Fund II Reports $86.9M First Close Against $200M Target
entry.summary: Motive Partners' second venture vehicle has secured $86.89 million against a $200 million target, reaching its first close in August 2026. Motive Venture Fund II, LP has reached its first close at $86.89 million, representing approximately 43.45% of its $200 million fundraising target. Launched in June 2025, the vehicle reached…
entry.content:
Motive Partners' second venture vehicle has secured $86.89 million against a $200 million target, reaching its first close in August 2026.

Motive Venture Fund II, LP has reached its first close at $86.89 million, representing approximately 43.45% of its $200 million fundraising target. Launched in June 2025, the vehicle reached the milestone in August 2026, with $113.11 million remaining against its stated offering.

Motive's venture investment platform

Founded in 2015 by Rob Heyvaert, Motive Partners is a New York-based investment firm focused on financial technology and technology-enabled business services. The firm invests across early-stage ventures, growth equity and buyouts, with an investment presence in North America and Europe.

Its venture platform, Motive Ventures, focuses on early-stage financial technology businesses, particularly companies developing solutions across wealth and asset management, banking, payments, insurance and capital markets. Its investment themes also extend to artificial intelligence, financial data infrastructure and embedded finance.

Motive's venture strategy targets companies from pre-seed to Series A, with typical lead or co-lead investments ranging between $1 million and $10 million. The broader investment platform also backs established businesses through growth and buyout transactions.

entry.title: Travel + Leisure Reported Better Loan Numbers. The SEC Says Cancelled Loans Helped.
entry.summary:
Wyndham Destinations reported an improving measure of timeshare loan losses in 2019. The SEC alleges that two undisclosed projects helped produce that improvement by removing delinquent and defaulted loans from the company’s portfolio.

On October 30, 2019, the company reported a Loan Loss Provision Percentage of 20.3% for the third quarter, down from 20.8% a year earlier. The SEC alleges the measure would not have improved year over year without the projects. The loan rescissions at issue ran from May 2019 to at least December 2020, so the total population spans a longer period than the third-quarter comparison.
entry.content:
Wyndham Destinations reported an improving measure of timeshare loan losses in 2019. The SEC alleges that two undisclosed projects helped produce that improvement by removing delinquent and defaulted loans from the company’s portfolio.

On October 30, 2019, the company reported a Loan Loss Provision Percentage of 20.3% for the third quarter, down from 20.8% a year earlier. The SEC alleges the measure would not have improved year over year without the projects. The loan rescissions at issue ran from May 2019 to at least December 2020, so the total population spans a longer period than the third-quarter comparison.

The number investors were watching

The Loan Loss Provision Percentage measured the provision for loan losses against gross vacation ownership interest sales, net of fee-for-service sales. It was one of the measures investors watched to assess the performance of the company’s timeshare loan portfolio.

By spring 2019, the percentage was moving in the wrong direction. Wyndham Destinations reported 22.5% for the first quarter, up from 20.4% a year earlier. According to the SEC’s complaint, five analysts questioned the increase on the May 1, 2019, first-quarter earnings call. Management said it would stop the year-over-year increases and achieve its 2019 guidance: a full-year percentage comparable to 2018, when it was 20.5%.

Two projects inside the business

The SEC alleges that the company ran two projects to rescind delinquent or defaulted timeshare loans: the Special Handling Project (SHP), which began in May 2019, and the Past-Due Project (PDP), which began in August.

Under the SHP, the company set targets for the number of delinquent or defaulted loans to rescind. Those targets were linked to its Loan Loss Provision Percentage guidance. They appeared in monthly forecasts from May 2019 through late 2020, with senior management agreeing on them at least quarterly.

The SHP focused on loans tied to customers whose earlier requests to rescind their timeshare contracts had been rejected or left unaddressed. The complaint says those requests had typically been rejected because they fell outside the statutory rescission period or because the sale complied with company policy.

The PDP used spreadsheets of delinquent and defaulted loans linked to customer complaints. According to the complaint, the Sales Reversal Committee approved the loans on those agendas in bulk, without reviewing each one individually.

Across both projects, the SEC alleges that more than 2,900 delinquent or defaulted loans were rescinded between May 2019 and at least December 2020. They carried about $77 million in outstanding loan balances, including roughly $34 million in defaulted loans.

How the accounting changed

The complaint says that once a contract was coded as rescinded, the company reversed the original revenue and the related Loan Loss Provision. For loans more than 120 days past due, it also reversed the defaulted amounts.

In effect, the company’s accounting system treated the original sale and resulting loan as though they had never happened.

The SEC alleges that, in several quarters in 2019 and 2020, the projects improved the Loan Loss Provision and Loan Loss Provision Percentage by “more than five percent.” The complaint does not make the basis of that phrase clear enough to translate it into percentage points or a relative percentage.

The complaint also says the company forecast the expected effects of the rescissions but did not track their actual impact on its financial statements.

What investors were told

On the third-quarter 2019 earnings call, company executives attributed improvements in loan-loss measures to operational initiatives, including customer-care efforts, stricter underwriting and changes to the reservation system. The SEC alleges those explanations omitted the contribution of the rescission projects.

For the full year, the company said it had kept the percentage flat year over year and met its guidance. The SEC alleges the undisclosed rescissions helped it achieve that outcome.

The complaint also links the alleged disclosure omissions to capital raising. During the relevant period, the company sold about $1.65 billion of notes in three private offerings that incorporated the filings the SEC alleges were misleading.

The settlement

On September 30, 2026, the SEC announced a settled action against Travel + Leisure Co., the company’s later name. Travel + Leisure consented to a final judgment with a $975,000 civil penalty and a bar on violating specified securities-law provisions, without admitting the allegations, subject to court approval. The company had disclosed the agreement in its second-quarter 2026 Form 10-Q and accrued the $975,000.

The allegations have not been tested at trial.

The SEC’s complaint describes a reported improvement, internal rescission targets and an accounting process that removed loans from the portfolio. The unresolved question is how much each project contributed to the reported measure.

Based on the SEC’s complaint and litigation release and the company’s filings reviewed for this article, through October 24, 2026.

entry.title: What Did Go-Ahead’s Auditor Miss?
entry.summary:
The FRC says two Go-Ahead rail subsidiaries wrongfully retained more than £30 million of public money. Its case against Deloitte covers five years of audits.

The £2.4 Million Release

According to the Financial Reporting Council (FRC), London & South Eastern Railway Ltd (LSER), the company behind Southeastern, released £2.4 million in overpayments into profit in its 2016 financial year without informing the Department for Transport (DfT).

Deloitte audited Go-Ahead Group, LSER’s parent, for that year and the four after it. What did the auditor ask about the money, the obligation to repay it and the way it appeared in the accounts?
entry.content:
The FRC says two Go-Ahead rail subsidiaries wrongfully retained more than £30 million of public money. Its case against Deloitte covers five years of audits.

The £2.4 Million Release

According to the Financial Reporting Council (FRC), London & South Eastern Railway Ltd (LSER), the company behind Southeastern, released £2.4 million in overpayments into profit in its 2016 financial year without informing the Department for Transport (DfT).

Deloitte audited Go-Ahead Group, LSER’s parent, for that year and the four after it. What did the auditor ask about the money, the obligation to repay it and the way it appeared in the accounts?

An Obligation That Stayed in the Accounts

LSER had received erroneous overpayments from the DfT before Deloitte became Go-Ahead’s auditor. The company was obliged to repay the money, recorded accruals against the amounts owed, and began releasing accruals into profit without informing the Department.

An accrual is an accounting entry that recognises an amount owed, even when the cash has not yet been paid. The FRC said LSER accrued a further £27 million from 2016 to 2020 under a subsequent franchise agreement. In its 2019 and 2020 financial statements, the accruals were classified in a way the FRC said disguised their true nature.

The issue was not simply that money had been received in error. Amounts owed to the Department remained in the accounts while some were released into profit.

What Management’s Evidence Suggested

The FRC said evidence obtained from LSER management during later audit years suggested the company intended to release overpayments under the subsequent franchise agreement into profit if the DfT did not discover them. The FRC’s announcement does not say whether that evidence reached Deloitte’s audit team.

A Second Subsidiary

The FRC identified a related issue at London & Birmingham Railway Ltd (LM), another Go-Ahead subsidiary. In its 2020 financial year, after its franchise ended, LM released £5.6 million of accruals to profit and attempted to conceal the release through the wording of a financial statement note, according to the FRC.

The cases involved separate subsidiaries and franchise agreements. The FRC described more than £30 million of public money as wrongfully retained by LSER and LM for an extended period.

How the Department Found Out

In July 2020, the DfT identified an indexation error in the calculation of HS1 track-access charges under LSER’s 2014 franchise agreement. The Department initially believed that profit-sharing arrangements would recover much of the overpayment.

In April 2021, the DfT required payment of amounts it believed were owed and sought a breakdown of creditor balances. In May, LSER told the Department that the overpaid subsidy was higher than the amount the DfT had identified and disclosed additional overpayments relating to HS1 depot rentals. LSER had accrued for both categories because it recognised they would need to be repaid.

LSER paid the principal amounts for the track-access and depot-rental overpayments in May 2021. In September 2021, the government announced that it would take over the Southeastern operation after the DfT identified more than £25 million in taxpayer funding that had not been declared.

By then LSER’s books already carried the liability. The Department was still working out how large it was.

The Figures

Figure What it represents
More than £30 million The FRC’s description of public money wrongfully retained by LSER and LM
More than £25 million Funding the DfT said LSER had not declared, behind its September 2021 action
£51.3 million due; £49.2 million paid Go-Ahead’s 2021 results: total owed to the DfT, including the previously disclosed £25 million, and what LSER had paid by publication
£23.5 million The DfT’s separate penalty on LSER for franchise breaches

The LSER Money Came Back. The Audit Remained.

The DfT’s annual report said the sums and interest associated with the LSER irregularities it had identified were recovered in full. The £23.5 million penalty was remitted to the Exchequer in May 2022.

The LSER money came back. The FRC’s case was about what the auditors did while it sat in the accounts.

The FRC found that Deloitte had failed to make sufficient enquiries into LSER’s and LM’s actions, apply adequate professional scepticism, evaluate evidence of fraud-risk factors and appreciate the contractual good-faith obligations involved. The FRC described the findings as a “highly concerning pattern of failure” to apply sufficient scrutiny.

The findings covered Deloitte’s audits of Go-Ahead’s consolidated financial statements for the financial years ended in 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2020. A separate finding concerned Go-Ahead Bayern GmbH, where the FRC said Deloitte did not sufficiently scrutinise changes to the contract-loss forecasts behind a provision.

The FRC fined Deloitte £6.05 million, reduced from £11 million after discounts for exceptional cooperation and admissions with early disposal. It also issued a severe reprimand, declared that the audit reports did not satisfy the relevant requirements, and required Deloitte to report to its FRC supervisor on root causes, remedial action and empirical evidence that the measures taken were effective.

Did the evidence of management’s intentions ever reach the people signing the audit reports?

Research boundary: Based on the FRC’s announcement of 8 October 2026, the DfT’s penalty notice, Go-Ahead’s results and the DfT’s annual report. The FRC’s full decision notice was not reviewed.

entry.title: The Capital Trail Inside Meyer Global
entry.summary:
On January 3, 2024, a Meyer Global-managed fund faced a $46,020 capital call tied to a SpaceX investment.

The call was not met.

The Securities and Exchange Commission says the result was the forfeiture of an investment worth nearly $3 million.

That gap — $46,020 owed against an investment valued at nearly $3 million — is where the Meyer Global story becomes larger than a single missed payment.
entry.content:
On January 3, 2024, a Meyer Global-managed fund faced a $46,020 capital call tied to a SpaceX investment.

The call was not met.

The Securities and Exchange Commission says the result was the forfeiture of an investment worth nearly $3 million.

That gap — $46,020 owed against an investment valued at nearly $3 million — is where the Meyer Global story becomes larger than a single missed payment.

The money had entered a network of private funds built to give investors access to companies such as SpaceX, OpenAI and other pre-IPO businesses. On September 30, 2026, the SEC alleged that some of the money moving through that network did not remain on the investment path.

This account follows those movements: from the funds investors were asked to join, into private-market investments, and then into the transactions described in the SEC's complaint.

Where a transaction is reported by a credible source rather than directly documented in the SEC filings, it is identified as such. Where the SEC is making an allegation, it is treated as an allegation.

The fund behind the SpaceX investment

The SEC says Owen E.H. Meyer began raising capital as early as November 2019 for private funds that would acquire interests in pre-IPO companies. The first vehicle was Starship I.

By the time described in the SEC complaint, Meyer Global Management — or MGM — had created approximately 16 affiliated private funds. The funds were generally designed around individual pre-IPO investments. Rather than always holding company shares directly, they could invest through another fund or adviser that held the underlying securities.

That structure helps explain why a SpaceX investment could sit several layers away from the individual who supplied the money.

SEC Form D filings show the machinery in pieces.

Starship X, for example, identifies Meyer Equity LLC as an executive officer and director and Owen Meyer as an executive officer, director, promoter and managing partner. Another filing for Starship 11 identifies Meyer Equity LLC as general partner and Owen Meyer as a related person.

The scale was larger than any one filing.

Bloomberg Law reported that the SEC alleges MGM raised at least $18.5 million from nearly 100 investors. An AUM13F record separately associates the manager or sponsor with 23 private funds. The SEC's complaint refers to approximately 16 affiliated funds. Those figures come from different records and descriptions of the fund universe; they do not, by themselves, establish that money is missing.

Some individual filings show capital entering the system.

Starship III reported $1,028,225 in securities sold. Starship IV reported $323,728. Starship 11 reported $564,702, while Destinus I reported $100,000.

Together, those four reported amounts total $2,016,655 — a calculation from selected filings, not a measure of MGM's total fundraising.

The investments were not confined to SpaceX

One of the funds was also connected to PlayStar Gaming Group AB.

In December 2022, PlayStar announced a $15 million investment, with reporting identifying Meyer Global as a minority investor. PlayStar said the funding would support its New Jersey operations and planned Pennsylvania expansion. 

The investment later encountered a different transaction.

Glitnor acquired a 37.5% stake in PlayStar.

If a Meyer-related fund held part of PlayStar when that transaction happened, what happened to that fund's position?

The investment and the later Glitnor transaction are documented. The complete economics of the Meyer vehicle's entry position, subsequent ownership and disposition are not.

That question becomes more interesting when the SEC's allegations are followed back into the accounts connected to the Meyer funds.

Then the money starts moving differently

The SEC alleges that, beginning at least in December 2021, Meyer and MGM misused assets from MGM-managed funds and misled investors. In one scheme, the SEC alleges that investor proceeds were diverted and that investors were required to sign releases accepting less than they were owed before receiving any money. In another, the SEC alleges that investor statements were inflated. 

Some of the transactions are unusually specific.

On April 12, the SEC alleges that $35,000 moved from an account associated with the PlayStar investment to Meyer's personal account.

Twelve days later, another $30,000 moved from the same PlayStar-related account to his personal account.

Then came a smaller transaction that makes the sequence unusually easy to follow.

A $4,415.56 charge at a strip club was attempted on a Meyer Global Partners card. The charge was declined. A $10,000 transfer was then made into the account, and the payment went through minutes later.

The SEC alleges these transactions as part of the broader misuse of fund assets. They are not adjudicated findings.

The complaint describes other transfers with similarly specific trails.

The SEC says Meyer transferred $636,000 from the Liquidated SpaceX Funds to a personal account. From that money, the complaint says, he spent thousands of dollars at Bloomingdale's and Amazon between November 2025 and February 2026.

Another $23,000 wire went to an individual with a memo referencing “Destinus Funding Investments.” Destinus was held by another MGM-managed fund, while the Liquidated SpaceX Funds did not invest in Destinus.

Between November 2025 and January 2026, the SEC says six additional wires totaling $40,000 went to another individual. The recipient, according to the complaint, was not an investor in the Liquidated SpaceX Funds.

In December 2025, another $86,000 went to Meyer's father. The memo included “Oikoi Network Fund – Return of Funds.” The SEC says Meyer's father was not an investor in the Liquidated SpaceX Funds. 

Taken together, these are not simply fund names appearing in a database. They are individual transfers: amounts, dates, recipients, account movements and, in several cases, transaction descriptions.

The SpaceX loss looks different when viewed alongside those transfers

Return to the $46,020 capital call.

The SEC alleges that an MGM-managed fund faced a capital-call deficiency connected to its SpaceX investment. The fund did not meet the call, and the SEC says the result was forfeiture of an investment worth nearly $3 million. 

A capital call is not itself unusual. Private-market investments can require a fund to supply additional capital after an initial commitment.

What matters here is what happened when that obligation was not met.

The SEC says the fund lost the SpaceX investment.

An obligation of $46,020 therefore stood between the fund and an asset that the SEC valued at nearly $3 million.

The underlying investment chain was more complicated than those two numbers suggest. The SEC says the funds could invest through other advisers or vehicles rather than directly holding every underlying security. 

The complete contractual sequence — the exact investment vehicle, original acquisition terms, capital-call notice, deadline, forfeiture provision and subsequent recipient of the interest — is not contained in the material reviewed for this investigation.

That last step matters because forfeiture tells us what happened to the fund's position. It does not, by itself, tell us who ended up with the economic interest.

The names become important again

The capital did not move through one entity called Meyer Global.

Meyer Equity LLC appears in fund filings. Oikoi Network Partners appears across multiple Starship vehicles. Meyer Global Management appears as the investment manager in regulatory records. Meyer Global GP LLC exists as a separate entity associated with the broader structure. 

The same problem appears in the PlayStar records.

One source refers to an MGP I fund, while other material refers to Meyer Global Partners. The available evidence does not establish that those names should automatically be treated as the same legal vehicle.

That distinction matters because the entity holding an investment is the entity whose economics have to be followed.

A brand name can tell you where to look.

The legal entity tells you where the asset sits.

Three trails, one unresolved question

The PlayStar investment is one trail: money raised, investment made, and a later transaction in which Glitnor acquired a 37.5% stake.

The SEC's alleged PlayStar-account transfers are another: $35,000, then $30,000, moving from the account associated with the investment into Meyer's personal account, followed by the strip-club payment sequence.

The SpaceX episode is a third: investment acquired, a $46,020 capital call issued, the obligation allegedly left unmet, and an interest worth nearly $3 million forfeited.

The SEC's other alleged transfers — including the $636,000 movement into Meyer's personal account, the $23,000 Destinus wire, the six $40,000 wires and the $86,000 payment to his father — add further points to the capital trail.

The transactions do not all have the same explanation. But they can be followed through the entities, accounts and investment vehicles named in the underlying records.

And at the end of the SpaceX trail, one question remains:

Who ultimately received the forfeited SpaceX interest, and on what terms?

entry.title: Mars FX’s $566.7 Million Withdrawal Request Raises a Basic Question: Who Actually Held the Assets?
entry.summary:
On November 11, 2024, Novus, acting on behalf of Mars FX Master Fund, asked for roughly $566.73 million to be withdrawn from a trading arrangement it believed represented the value of its investment.

The request covered 2,250 trading accounts held in the name of Mars FX Master Fund, according to restructuring materials now before courts in the United States and the British Virgin Islands. The deadline was January 30, 2025. The money was not paid.

Within weeks, Mars FX told investors that it could no longer operate in the ordinary course. The Cayman entities suspended redemptions. The group eventually entered insolvency proceedings.

Today, the $566.73 million figure sits at the centre of a much harder question.
entry.content:
On November 11, 2024, Novus, acting on behalf of Mars FX Master Fund, asked for roughly $566.73 million to be withdrawn from a trading arrangement it believed represented the value of its investment.

The request covered 2,250 trading accounts held in the name of Mars FX Master Fund, according to restructuring materials now before courts in the United States and the British Virgin Islands. The deadline was January 30, 2025. The money was not paid.

Within weeks, Mars FX told investors that it could no longer operate in the ordinary course. The Cayman entities suspended redemptions. The group eventually entered insolvency proceedings.

Today, the $566.73 million figure sits at the centre of a much harder question.

What, exactly, did that number represent — and where were the underlying assets actually held?

The answer matters because the documents do not describe a simple structure in which Mars FX held $566.73 million in a bank or brokerage account in its own name. They describe a chain involving a U.S. feeder fund, a Cayman master fund, Hong Kong banks and trust companies, a trading-platform operator, and brokerage accounts held in the names of entities connected to that operator.

The distinction between those things — an investment value, a platform balance, a legal account, and independently verified assets — is where this story becomes difficult.

The money started with a conventional fund structure

Mars FX US LP was formed in Delaware in 2020 as the U.S. vehicle in a master-feeder structure. Its 2024 SEC Form D amendment reported that the partnership had sold $331.08 million of fund interests to 426 investors, up from $239.32 million in 2023, $146.64 million in 2022 and $44.37 million in 2021. The filing identifies Novus Capital Partners LLC as the fund's general partner and names David Choi, Ashish Patel, Patrick Hofmann and Jae Y. Choi among the related persons.

A Form D is not an SEC audit of a fund. The SEC's filing itself states that the Commission has not necessarily reviewed the information or determined that it is accurate and complete.

The structure itself was straightforward enough. The movement of capital was more complicated.

Mars FX US was the onshore feeder. Mars FX International was the offshore feeder. Mars FX Master Ltd, in the Cayman Islands, was the master fund through which the trading strategy was supposed to operate. Novus served as general partner of the U.S. vehicle and investment manager of the Cayman entities. A January 31, 2025 shareholder register recorded Mars FX US as owning 75.64% of the Master Fund, represented by 1,464,828.2367 Class A shares at a stated NAV price of $296.4860 per share, or approximately $434.3 million.

$277 million was sent into the trading arrangement

According to materials summarised in the Mars FX Chapter 11 record, the U.S. debtor and the two Cayman entities collectively invested approximately $277.371 million into a trading structure operated by Tech RealFX Ltd., or TRFX, between August 2020 and August 2024.

The available reconstruction identifies two major routes from the U.S. fund into Hong Kong.

Between August 2, 2020 and February 25, 2025, Mars FX transferred approximately $122.336 million from accounts at JPMorgan Chase and Northern Trust to Bank of Communications (Hong Kong).

Between April 7, 2022 and August 1, 2024, it transferred another $131.25 million from Northern Trust to accounts at Legacy Trust Company in Hong Kong.

Those two numbers total approximately $253.6 million. They should not, however, simply be treated as a second, independent measure of money invested. The materials describe them as historical transfers over overlapping periods, while the $277.371 million figure is described as the collective investment of the debtor and Cayman entities. Without the complete bank ledger and transaction-level reconciliation, the gross transfer totals cannot safely be treated as a clean measure of unique capital deployed.

That distinction is important because the documentary trail does not yet produce a single, perfectly reconciled line that can be labelled “investor money in” and another that can be labelled “money out.”

Instead, it produces a chain.

Investors → Mars FX entities → JPMorgan / Northern Trust → BOCOM / Legacy Trust → TRFX-related structure → brokerage accounts → reported trading balance.

The brokerage accounts were not in the Master Fund’s name

This is one of the most consequential details in the record.

The restructuring materials identify brokerage accounts at Equiti Capital UK and GO Markets. But the accounts were held in the names of TRFX, 4XHUB Limited and Treal Capital Limited, rather than directly in the name of Mars FX Master Ltd. Trading from those accounts was understood to have taken place through TRFX's technology platform.

That creates a distinction between the person or entity named on an account and the party asserting an economic entitlement to the assets in that account.

The Mars FX materials say that certain balances in those accounts may have been held for the benefit of the Master Fund and, indirectly, the U.S. feeder. But the same materials say that the beneficial ownership of the relevant bank, trust and brokerage accounts remains under investigation.

There is another layer of uncertainty. The available records identify similarly named companies across jurisdictions, including TRFX and Treal entities in the BVI and Hong Kong and 4XHUB entities in Labuan and Hong Kong. The restructuring record says investigations are continuing into which legal entities actually owned the relevant accounts.

In other words, the question is not simply whether money entered a trading platform.

It is also:

Whose account was it in?
Who had legal title?
Who had beneficial ownership?
And who could actually withdraw it?

Those are different questions.

Then came the $566.73 million withdrawal request

The number that eventually brought the structure into focus was substantially larger than the roughly $277.4 million described as cumulative investment into the TRFX trading arrangement.

On November 11, 2024, Novus, acting on behalf of the Master Fund, submitted a withdrawal request seeking approximately $566.73 million covering all 2,250 trading accounts described as being held in the name of the Master Fund. The amount represented the claimed platform balance, including purported trading profits. The requested payment deadline was January 30, 2025.

That makes the $566.73 million figure specific to the Mars FX Master Fund's asserted position. It is not presented in the restructuring record as the total value of TRFX's entire client platform.

But specificity does not make it cash.

A withdrawal request demonstrates that Mars FX asserted an entitlement to a particular amount. It does not, by itself, establish that $566.73 million existed as withdrawable cash in an independently verified account.

The gap between those two propositions is the central evidentiary issue.

The number was represented as an asset before it became a disputed claim

The earlier audited financial statements make the issue more difficult.

The Master Fund's 2022 financial statements reported $248.09 million of total cash at bank and broker. The corresponding 2023 figure was $381.35 million.

For Mars FX US, the investment in the Master Fund was recorded at fair value of $207.35 million in 2022 and $325.27 million in 2023, accompanied by cash at bank of $8.56 million and $7.32 million respectively. The audit reports for those years were unqualified, according to the restructuring materials.

Those statements matter because they show that substantial assets were being reported through the fund's accounting system before the withdrawal failure.

They do not, by themselves, answer where the economic assets were sitting in the external financial system.

The distinction became particularly important because the liquidators later began investigating the audit process itself.

The restructuring record says the Joint Official Liquidators are investigating potential professional-negligence and breach-of-contract claims against Deloitte relating to the 2022 and 2023 audits. It also says there is a sufficient basis, on the information then available, to investigate whether audit work adequately verified balances represented as being held with brokers or through associated material.

That is an investigation, not a finding that Deloitte failed in its duties.

And the later court order seeking Deloitte's records is likewise not a finding of wrongdoing. In the Mars FX Master Chapter 15 case, a U.S. Bankruptcy Court order entered on August 3, 2026 authorised the foreign representatives to issue subpoenas and examine Deloitte & Touche in connection with the restructuring.

What the audit records ultimately establish remains an open question.

The documents also disagree about what happened at TRFX

The legal dispute with TRFX adds another layer.

After the withdrawal request went unpaid, statutory demands were served in February 2025. TRFX subsequently challenged the underlying arrangements, arguing, among other things, that agreements had been executed by an individual who lacked authority, that certain correspondence and broker statements relied upon by Mars FX were forged, and that there was no evidence that the Master Fund had transferred the relevant funds to TRFX.

That application was later discontinued.

Mars FX and the Cayman entities then commenced BVI proceedings seeking recovery of approximately $566.73 million. TRFX's defence, filed in November 2025, disputed the authenticity or authority underlying key documents, denied receiving or holding client monies and advanced a materially different account of the trading history and balances. The proceedings remain ongoing.

One particularly important allegation concerns TRFX's platform itself. The restructuring materials note unresolved questions around a change in the website domain hosting the trading platform around October 2022 and competing accounts concerning operational control.

None of that establishes that the reported trading results were fictitious.

It does establish something narrower and more useful: the parties now disagree materially about the underlying agreements, authority, custody and trading history that support the claimed balance.

Those disagreements have to be resolved through documents and external records, not inferred from the size of the final number.

The balance sheet now tells a different story

By January 31, 2025, the Master Fund's shareholder register recorded Mars FX US's 75.64% interest at $434.3 million. The investor register for Mars FX US recorded approximately $432.63 million of aggregate investor NAV across 535 positions.

At first glance, those numbers can appear connected to the $566.73 million withdrawal request, but they measure different things at different points in time.

The $434.3 million figure is the recorded value of Mars FX US's stake in the Master Fund.

The $432.63 million figure is the recorded aggregate NAV of the U.S. vehicle's investors.

The $566.73 million figure is the claimed combined platform position that Novus sought to withdraw on behalf of the Master Fund in November 2024.

And the approximately $277.37 million figure describes cumulative investment by the debtor and Cayman entities into the TRFX trading arrangement through August 2024.

These numbers should not be forced into a single reconciliation before the underlying records support one.

What they do show is the scale of the problem. A capital deployment of roughly $277 million was associated with a reported platform position of roughly $567 million. That difference is not automatically unexplained money, and it is not automatically proven trading profit. It represents a claimed economic increase whose underlying transaction and valuation history now matters.

The question is whether the documentary record can bridge those numbers.

What is independently established — and what is not

The Mars FX case now sits inside several legal systems at once.

The U.S. Chapter 11 case for Mars FX US was filed on March 23, 2026. On September 21, 2026, the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York entered an order confirming Mars FX US's First Amended Plan of Liquidation.

The Cayman Master Fund is proceeding under Chapter 15 recognition proceedings in the same court, alongside the Cayman liquidation process. The BVI litigation against TRFX remains a principal recovery route.

The practical task for the estate is therefore not merely to determine whether a number appeared in a financial statement.

It is to reconstruct the chain from the original capital to whatever assets, claims or rights remain recoverable today.

That reconstruction requires several separate answers. There must be bank records showing what left Mars FX accounts. There must be records showing what arrived at BOCOM and Legacy Trust. There must be documents establishing which legal entities controlled the receiving accounts. There must be broker statements and broker-side records establishing what Equiti and GO Markets actually held. There must be evidence establishing who owned those brokerage balances. And there must be sufficient audit documentation to establish what evidence was available to the auditors when the 2022 and 2023 balances were reported. Only after those steps can the economic story be completed.

The unanswered question is narrower than “where did the money go?”

That broader question assumes the money disappeared in a particular way.

The records available today do not establish that.

The more precise question is harder — and potentially more revealing:

At each stage between Mars FX's investors and the claimed $566.73 million platform balance, what asset or contractual right existed, who legally controlled it, and what independent evidence verified it?

The distinction matters. Investor capital can become a fund interest. A fund interest can become an investment recorded at fair value. A fund can assert a claim against a trading counterparty. A trading platform can report an account balance. A broker can maintain an account in another entity's name. And an auditor can receive evidence purporting to support a balance.

Those statements can all be true at the same time without establishing that the final economic asset was readily recoverable by the investor.

That is the problem Mars FX is now trying to solve through liquidation, litigation and discovery.

The $566.73 million figure is therefore best understood not as the end of the investigation, but as the beginning of it.

The courts will ultimately determine the legal claims. The brokers and other record holders may provide the transaction history. The audit records may clarify what was independently checked and how.

For now, the restructuring record reviewed here reports a large claimed asset position, substantial historical transfers and a complicated custody structure.

It does not yet provide a complete, independently verified bridge from one to the other.

That bridge is the missing piece.

entry.title: Where Did NFE's $5.7 Billion Go?
entry.summary:
On September 11, 2026, New Fortress Energy completed its restructuring. The headline was easy to understand: roughly $5.7 billion of third-party debt had been extinguished, leaving the company with about $700 million of corporate debt.

Then you look at what happened to the claims behind that debt. The first surprise is Brazil: NFE had separated its Brazilian operations into a new entity, BrazilCo, and at closing 100% of BrazilCo's common equity went to the plan creditors.

So the restructuring wasn't just about reducing what NFE owed. It also changed who owned part of the business, and Brazil was only the beginning.
entry.content:
On September 11, 2026, New Fortress Energy completed its restructuring. The headline was easy to understand: roughly $5.7 billion of third-party debt had been extinguished, leaving the company with about $700 million of corporate debt.

Then you look at what happened to the claims behind that debt. The first surprise is Brazil: NFE had separated its Brazilian operations into a new entity, BrazilCo, and at closing 100% of BrazilCo's common equity went to the plan creditors.

So the restructuring wasn't just about reducing what NFE owed. It also changed who owned part of the business, and Brazil was only the beginning.

The creditors didn't just get their old claims back

The reorganized CoreCo issued $571.3 million of new senior secured term loans to plan creditors. It also issued 2,454,936 Series A mandatorily convertible preferred shares, with an aggregate liquidation preference of $2.4549 billion, along with 10,608,922 shares of CoreCo common stock, representing 65% of CoreCo's common stock at closing.

The plan creditors had become something else: part lender, part preferred investor, part common shareholder and, through BrazilCo, owners of an entire operating business.

That changes the question. A debt claim has a face value and repayment priority; common equity participates in whatever value remains, while preferred equity sits somewhere between those positions with its own rights and conversion mechanics.

Putting those instruments into one headline recovery number would hide more than it reveals.

Then the company split again

There was another layer to the restructuring. FLNG 2 was placed into a separate financing structure for a separate creditor group, with $400 million of non-recourse term loans and $200 million of preferred equity. That $400 million is project-level, non-recourse financing and sits outside the roughly $700 million of corporate debt described above.

Instead of dividing one pool of securities among creditors, the transaction divided the enterprise itself. BrazilCo became one pool of assets and ownership, the continuing CoreCo business another, while FLNG 2 carried its own financing structure.

Different creditors could therefore emerge with exposure to very different parts of what had once been one NFE group. That is a much bigger change than a lower debt balance.

And NFE was still raising money

While the old capital structure was being dismantled, the new one was also being funded. NFE raised $136.5 million of new financing at closing.

The pro forma disclosure shows the detail underneath that figure: a $36.5 million senior term loan was reduced by a $1.5 million original-issue discount to $35 million of net proceeds, alongside $100 million of junior term loans. The resulting $135 million of cash proceeds was therefore lower than the $136.5 million face amount of the financing.

The company was reducing old obligations, changing ownership, creating new securities and bringing in fresh capital at the same time. This was a reconstruction of the capital structure, not just a reduction in it.

The interesting part is what the debt reduction changed

Before the restructuring, NFE's creditors were primarily looking at claims for repayment. After it, part of that exposure had become ownership, with the plan creditors holding the entire equity of BrazilCo and a majority of the common stock of the reorganized CoreCo at closing, alongside preferred equity and new secured debt.

Existing shareholders, meanwhile, were left with the residual common equity position beneath that new structure. The balance sheet had changed, but so had the map of who was exposed to which assets, and once that happens, the $5.7 billion headline becomes only the first number in the story.

Because a dollar of debt is not the same as a dollar of equity

This is where the restructuring becomes difficult to value. The new securities do not all carry the same economics: the term loan has contractual repayment terms and security, the preferred stake has its own priority and conversion mechanics, the common position participates in the residual value of CoreCo, and the Brazilian equity represents ownership of a separate operating business.

The FLNG 2 financing adds another layer because its claims are tied to a specific project structure rather than the wider CoreCo enterprise. The legal documents tell us what creditors received; they do not automatically tell us what all of those claims were worth.

That is where the restructuring stops being a balance-sheet story and starts becoming a valuation story.

Brazil is the number I would watch

NFE spent years building and acquiring a Brazilian LNG and power platform. At restructuring, that business was separated and its equity transferred to the creditors.

The transfer itself is clear. The harder question is sitting underneath it: what was BrazilCo actually worth when that equity changed hands?

That number would put the $5.7 billion debt reduction into a very different perspective.

entry.title: The AI Trade Had a Second Side: Inside the Rise and Unwind of Situational Awareness
entry.summary:
How a young AI-focused fund built a multibillion-dollar portfolio around the infrastructure boom — and what became visible when the trade had to unwind.

In July 2026, Citadel began buying a portfolio that had taken Situational Awareness less than two years to build.

The seller was not an old hedge fund caught on the wrong side of a trade. Situational Awareness had been founded in 2024 by Leopold Aschenbrenner, a former OpenAI employee who built the fund around a straightforward thesis: the consequences of artificial intelligence would extend far beyond software. The companies supplying chips, electricity, cooling, networking and computing capacity could become some of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom.
entry.content:
How a young AI-focused fund built a multibillion-dollar portfolio around the infrastructure boom — and what became visible when the trade had to unwind.

In July 2026, Citadel began buying a portfolio that had taken Situational Awareness less than two years to build.

The seller was not an old hedge fund caught on the wrong side of a trade. Situational Awareness had been founded in 2024 by Leopold Aschenbrenner, a former OpenAI employee who built the fund around a straightforward thesis: the consequences of artificial intelligence would extend far beyond software. The companies supplying chips, electricity, cooling, networking and computing capacity could become some of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom.

That bet attracted capital quickly.

By the middle of 2026, Situational Awareness was reporting more than $20 billion of reportable securities in its latest 13F filing.

Then the AI trade turned.

The portfolio that had been assembled around the expansion of AI infrastructure became one of the largest forced-position stories of the summer. Reports described financing pressure around the fund, JPMorgan curtailing lending, and Citadel taking on most of the stock portfolio.

The interesting part is not simply that a large fund lost money.

It is how the trade got that large in the first place — and what the unwind reveals about the financial machinery underneath the AI boom.

1. The Fund That Came Out of Nowhere

Situational Awareness appeared in public filings in 2024.

Its first onshore fund filing was made in September of that year, with the first sale reported on November 1. By September 2025, a Form D amendment showed roughly $998 million sold.

Six months later, a March 2026 amendment put the figure at approximately $1.76 billion, across 93 investors.

The adviser kept growing.

Its June 2026 ADV reported roughly $9.28 billion in regulatory assets under management.

The public securities portfolio was expanding even faster.

The 13F filing for the end of 2024 showed roughly $255 million in reportable securities.

Then:

$1.01 billion in Q1 2025.
$2.12 billion in Q2.
$4.14 billion in Q3.
$5.52 billion in Q4.

By Q1 2026, the filing had reached approximately $13.68 billion.

The Q2 filing, submitted in August, showed approximately $20.24 billion.

A fund founded in 2024 had, in less than two years, become a multibillion-dollar public-market operation.

And the portfolio gave away something about how Aschenbrenner viewed the AI cycle.

2. It Wasn't Really a Bet on AI Companies

The first holdings did not look like a conventional software portfolio.

There was Marvell, Vertiv, Vistra, Talen Energy, Constellation Energy, Modine.

The companies sat at very different points in the market, but they shared something: each had a relationship to the physical buildout required for more computing.

Power generation, Data-centre equipment, Cooling, Networking, Semiconductors, Infrastructure.

As the portfolio expanded, the theme became broader. CoreWeave appeared.

So did Core Scientific, Applied Digital, IREN, Bloom Energy, Coherent, Lumentum, Riot Platforms, Sandisk and TSMC.

The portfolio also moved into semiconductor names and options, including positions tied to Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom, AMD, Oracle, ASML and other parts of the semiconductor chain.

This made the original thesis clearer.

The bet was not simply that AI companies would make more money.

It was that the world would have to spend extraordinary amounts of money to build the machinery needed for AI. That meant the opportunity could sit one step below the headline companies.

A data-centre operator could benefit. So could a power producer. A networking company. A chip manufacturer. A cooling supplier. A company controlling access to computing capacity.

The portfolio was beginning to look less like an AI stock basket and more like a map of the infrastructure boom.

Then the options complicated the picture again.

3. The Fund Wasn't Just Buying the Winners

By 2025, Situational Awareness was also using derivatives to express views around the semiconductor complex.

The quarterly filings included large put positions.

Secondary analysis of the Q1 2026 filing estimated approximately $8.46 billion of semiconductor put exposure across names including SMH, Nvidia, Broadcom, AMD, Oracle, ASML, TSMC and Micron.

Those positions could have served different purposes inside a much larger portfolio: downside bets, hedges, or part of more complex combinations.

But one thing was clear from the filings.

The fund was not simply buying companies that stood to benefit from AI spending and holding them.

It was trading around the consequences of the same cycle. That distinction became important as the portfolio grew. A long position can be explained by a company's expected earnings. A portfolio combining infrastructure stocks with large option positions raises a different question:

How was the whole thing being financed?

4. The Part You Couldn't See in the 13F

A 13F tells you what securities were reportable at a particular moment.

It does not show the entire financial life of a fund. That distinction becomes much more interesting once the portfolio is measured in tens of billions.

Reports around Situational Awareness's 2026 stress described relationships with Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Citigroup and Bank of America, followed later by a prime-brokerage relationship with Clear Street.

The financing itself remained behind the portfolio.

Which securities were pledged?

How much borrowing sat against them?

How much room existed before a lender demanded more collateral?

And when the market started moving quickly, which part of the structure came under pressure first?

Those questions are usually invisible when looking at a quarterly holdings report.

The July episode brought them much closer to the surface.

Reuters reported that JPMorgan curtailed lending to the fund after losses tied to its AI positions.

Bloomberg reported that Situational Awareness established a relationship with Clear Street after the near-collapse of its leveraged AI positions.

Other reporting placed the fund's peak exposure at roughly $45 billion and described leverage of around 4×.

Those figures are secondary reports rather than a public financing ledger.

But they change the way the 13F should be read.

A $20 billion securities portfolio and $20 billion of investor capital are not the same thing. And a portfolio financed partly through borrowing behaves differently when the market moves sharply in the wrong direction.

5. The Companies Underneath the Trade Were Leveraged Too

There was another layer.

The same AI boom that drove investors into infrastructure companies was encouraging those companies to borrow heavily to build the infrastructure itself.

CoreWeave is the clearest example.

By June 2026, CoreWeave reported approximately $35.6 billion of debt and $103.7 billion of remaining performance obligations.

Earlier SEC filings showed an $8.5 billion delayed-draw term loan facility, secured by infrastructure including GPU servers.

The business model was increasingly turning expected future demand for computing into financing capacity today.

Customers commit to computing. Those commitments support revenue expectations. Infrastructure gets built. The infrastructure provides collateral. The collateral supports borrowing. And the borrowing funds still more infrastructure.

That is one reason CoreWeave is useful for understanding the financial side of the AI buildout. The company's growth story was not just an equity story. It was also a debt story.

Nebius provides another example. Its filings disclosed a $775 million senior secured term loan backed by GPU infrastructure and contracted cash flows. The company later raised approximately $4.34 billion in convertible debt.

Applied Digital disclosed $1.59 billion of senior secured notes to fund its Polaris Forge 1 data-centre project, alongside additional secured financing.

Different companies. Different structures. Same broader cycle.

The investor sees an AI infrastructure stock. The company sees an opportunity to borrow against infrastructure and future cash flows.

The lender sees collateral. The customer sees computing capacity.

And underneath all of them is the assumption that demand for AI infrastructure will continue to expand.

6. Then the Market Turned

That assumption became much harder to take for granted in July. The AI-related selloff hit companies across the ecosystem at the same time.

For an ordinary investor, falling prices mean a smaller portfolio. For a leveraged investor, falling prices can also mean shrinking collateral.

That difference is crucial.

A position can remain fundamentally attractive and still become a financing problem if its market value falls quickly enough.

Situational Awareness had built positions around exactly the part of the market that had expanded most aggressively.

Now the direction had changed.

JPMorgan's lending relationship was reportedly curtailed.

The fund's public portfolio was under pressure. And suddenly the question was no longer what those individual stocks were worth over the next five years.

It was who could take the entire position now.

7. Citadel Takes the Other Side

The answer, at least for much of the public-equity portfolio, was Citadel.

Reuters reported on July 30 that Citadel bought most of Situational Awareness's stock holdings after the AI rout. The reported value of the portfolio was around $16 billion.

That number is easy to misunderstand. It was the reported value of the public-equity book involved in the transaction — not an established purchase price.

The difference matters.

A portfolio can have a market value of $16 billion and still change hands for less if the seller needs immediate liquidity. And that appears to be what made the transaction unusual.

The reported discount to prevailing market prices was not merely a side detail. It was the price of moving a huge amount of risk quickly.

Later, Ken Griffin said Citadel had reduced more than 80% of the aggregate risk it had taken on and had executed roughly 100 block trades, representing more than $4 billion in value.

That gives the transaction a different character. Citadel was not simply “buying stocks.”

It was taking a large, concentrated bundle of market risk and then breaking it apart again.

The seller needed certainty. The buyer needed room to manage the positions. The gap between those two needs is where the discount lives. And that is where the cost of a forced unwind becomes visible.

8. What Had Been Built Was Bigger Than a Stock Portfolio

Look backward from that transaction and the pieces begin to line up.

A fund raises capital. It builds positions in companies positioned around AI infrastructure. It adds derivatives around parts of the semiconductor chain. Those positions sit inside a financing system involving prime brokers and lenders.

The companies underneath the positions are themselves raising billions against GPUs, data centres, contracted revenues and other infrastructure.

Then the market turns. Stock prices fall. Collateral values change. Financing becomes more important.

And a portfolio that had been accumulated over months needs to move in a matter of days.

From one angle, it is a hedge-fund liquidation. From another, it is a stress test of the entire financing chain around the AI boom.

That is what makes the Situational Awareness case unusually revealing. The fund did not create the AI capital cycle. It sat inside it.

9. The Unwind Changes the Way the AI Boom Looks

For most of the boom, the public story was straightforward.

AI demand was rising. Companies needed more chips. More chips required more data centres. Data centres required electricity, cooling, networking and land. Investors found the companies selling those things.

The financial side was less visible.

Capital was also being used to finance the infrastructure. Debt was being raised against assets. Future contracts were being turned into borrowing capacity. Prime brokers were financing market positions.

And large investors were using derivatives to express views on where the cycle might overheat.

None of those pieces needed to move together every day. But they were connected.

Situational Awareness became interesting precisely because the connections became visible when they were put under pressure.

The $20.24 billion 13F was the visible portfolio.

The reported ~$45 billion peak exposure points to something larger around it.

The $9.28 billion regulatory AUM belongs to yet another measurement.

The ~$16 billion Citadel transaction value describes the public-equity book at a particular moment.

They are not interchangeable numbers.

Together, they describe an investment operation whose public footprint had become much larger and more complicated than a simple list of stocks would suggest.

10. The Question Left Behind

Situational Awareness began with a view about where artificial intelligence was going. The fund found a way to express that view across power, chips, data centres, compute and the companies building them.

Capital followed. The portfolio expanded. Financing became part of the picture.

Then the same market that had rewarded the trade turned against it.

By the time Citadel was buying the portfolio, the story was no longer simply about which AI companies were going to win. It was about who could absorb the risk when the market stopped making room for everyone at once.

That is the part of the AI boom that a holdings report cannot show on its own.

The visible trade was in the stocks. The bigger trade was in the capital supporting everything underneath them.

Research boundary: This investigation uses the public evidence available through September 14, 2026. The precise lender-by-lender financing, collateral terms, margin mechanics and final economics of the Citadel transaction remain outside the public record used here. No finding of misconduct is made.

entry.title: What Was Backing Prax's Money?
entry.summary: Prax's expansion was accompanied by a series of increasingly large and more complex securitisation arrangements. The public record shows several stages in that financing programme: a US$750 million securitisation facility announced in 2021, a facility increased from £575 million to £739 million in 2022, and an arrangement described by Prax…
entry.content:
Prax's expansion was accompanied by a series of increasingly large and more complex securitisation arrangements.

The public record shows several stages in that financing programme: a US$750 million securitisation facility announced in 2021, a facility increased from £575 million to £739 million in 2022, and an arrangement described by Prax as a $1 billion securitisation facility in 2023. These figures should not be added together. The available record does not yet establish exactly how the facilities relate to one another.

Then State Oil, the parent company behind Prax, entered administration in 2025.

Administrators later reported material irregularities connected with a major receivables facility. Public reporting described a facility of roughly £783 million and a large gap between the amounts drawn and the receivables or invoices that were supposed to support them.

The obvious question is what happened to the money.

The more useful question comes earlier:

What was actually backing it?

A financing structure built alongside the expansion

Prax's financing story accelerated alongside the group's expansion.

In 2021, Prax acquired the Lindsey Oil Refinery and associated logistics assets from Total. Trafigura subsequently announced an exclusive arrangement to supply crude oil and refinery feedstock to Lindsey.

That same year, Prax announced a US$750 million securitisation facility.

The following year, Prax announced that its securitisation facility had been increased from £575 million to £739 million. HSBC, Citi, JPMorgan Chase and Royal Bank of Canada were identified as senior note purchasers.

In June 2023, Prax announced an extension and amendment of what it described as a $1 billion securitisation facility. The arrangement was extended to February 2025 and additional Prax entities in Switzerland, Singapore and the United States were brought into the structure.

A year later, Prax announced another facility: US$750 million of securitisation financing.

How the structure worked

The structure was built around Prax Global Financial Services DAC, an Irish special-purpose vehicle.

Under the disclosed structure, several Prax entities sold trade receivables — money owed to those businesses by customers — into the arrangement. The SPV then issued securities to financial institutions.

A receivables securitisation uses an underlying pool of receivables as part of the financing structure. The quality, eligibility and collection of those receivables therefore matter to the financing itself.

That is why the events of 2025 are important.

The paper trail shortly before the collapse

There is a useful glimpse of the structure in records of the International Stock Exchange (TISE).

An October 2024 notice reported aggregate senior notes of approximately £422.3 million and mezzanine notes of approximately £39.6 million associated with Prax Global Financial Services DAC. The corrected senior-note figure was £422,289,894, while the mezzanine notes were £39,647,589.

Senior and mezzanine notes are different layers of the financing structure: senior notes sit higher in the repayment hierarchy, while mezzanine notes take more risk.

Those figures should not be treated as a simple replacement for the earlier £739 million or $1 billion figures.

The public record currently does not establish that these amounts represent a single borrowing stack moving neatly from one size to another. Some may reflect different stages, currencies, note classes or related facilities.

The first task in understanding Prax's financing is therefore not to add the headline numbers together. It is to reconstruct the structure.

The gap reported after the collapse

That reconstruction looks very different after the 2025 administration.

Administrators reported material irregularities involving a major receivables facility. Global Trade Review reported a large gap between the facility's drawings and the receivables or invoices supporting those drawings. The final lender loss was not publicly quantified in the material available to the investigation.

The Guardian separately reported on a £783 million facility secured against expected oil-product sales and described irregularities identified by administrators.

That changes the significance of the earlier disclosures.

The financing announcements were public. The SPV was identifiable. The note structure was visible. The expansion of the financing programme was visible.

What those announcements did not reveal, at least from the material currently available, was the full quality and composition of the receivables supporting the financing.

What the public record can show

The existing documents allow part of the structure to be reconstructed: there was an operating group, receivables generated by multiple entities, a special-purpose vehicle into which those receivables fed, and securities issued by the SPV and purchased by international financial institutions.

The financing structure was repeatedly amended and expanded as Prax grew. After the group's collapse, administrators reported material irregularities in a major facility connected with that financing structure.

That makes the financing structure an important part of the story of Prax's collapse.

The administrators' account also points to refinery downtime, lower refining margins, heavy capital outlays and tax pressure as contributors to the group's deteriorating financial position.

But it is not enough to answer every question.

What remains unresolved

The available public material does not yet establish the exact receivables pool behind the facility, the advance rate, the complete eligibility tests applied to invoices, or exactly how collection accounts were controlled. It also does not provide a definitive public figure for the alleged shortfall.

The public record does not yet establish precisely how the £783 million facility referred to in administrator reporting relates to every earlier and later securitisation disclosure.

Those are not minor technicalities.

They are the difference between knowing that a financing structure existed and knowing exactly how it worked.

The audit trail

The financing questions are also why the Financial Reporting Council's September 2026 announcement matters.

The FRC opened an investigation into an individual accountant's conduct concerning State Oil's financing arrangements from February 2021 through June 2025. It also opened investigations into KPMG's audits of State Oil for the years ended February 2022 and February 2023, and PKF Littlejohn's audit for the year ended February 2024.

The announcement does not disclose the regulator's conclusions.

The FRC investigation therefore should not be treated as evidence that the auditors failed, or that misconduct has been established.

What it does establish is narrower:

the financing arrangements and the financial reporting around them are now the subject of formal regulatory scrutiny.

What Prax's public record leaves us with

The most useful way to understand the Prax collapse may not be to start with the collapse itself.

It is to look at the financing structure that preceded it.

Between 2021 and 2024, Prax publicly described a securitisation programme that became larger, more international and more complex. Behind that programme sat an SPV and receivables generated by operating entities. By 2025, administrators were reporting material irregularities in a major facility connected with those receivables.

The public record can show much of the architecture.

It cannot yet fully show what happened inside it.

entry.title: Northann Filed an Audit Opinion Its Auditor Says It Never Authorized
entry.summary: Northann Corp.'s annual report contained something investors normally take for granted: an auditor's opinion. The auditor later said it had never authorized it. Northann filed its FY2025 Form 10-K with the SEC on April 14, 2026. The filing presented financial statements accompanied by an audit report attributed to LAO Professionals.
entry.content:
Northann Corp.'s annual report contained something investors normally take for granted: an auditor's opinion.

The auditor later said it had never authorized it.

Northann filed its FY2025 Form 10-K with the SEC on April 14, 2026. The filing presented financial statements accompanied by an audit report attributed to LAO Professionals.

Later, the accounting firm said the document did not represent its work.

In a letter filed with the SEC, LAO said it had resigned on June 8 because its name and audit opinion had been used without authorization. The firm said it had not prepared, issued, signed, authorized or consented to the audit opinion included in Northann's filing.

That creates a question more basic than whether one particular number in Northann's accounts was wrong:

How did an audit opinion attributed to an accounting firm enter a public filing when the firm says it never authorized it?

The answer is not established by the current record. But the consequences are.

The audit had not been completed

LAO's later filing adds an important detail.

The firm said it had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to complete the audit or issue an opinion. According to LAO, it repeatedly requested documents needed to perform its procedures. LAO said Northann provided inaccessible links and declined requests to send certain large document sets as email attachments.

This was not a case of an auditor completing its work and later discovering an error in the accounts. According to LAO, the audit itself had not been completed.

Northann subsequently disclosed that LAO had not identified specific financial-statement items as incorrect. But because of LAO's statements about the audit report, Northann told investors not to rely on its FY2024 and FY2025 financial statements pending a new audit.

The distinction matters: the current evidence establishes a dispute over the audit process and authorization of the report. It does not, by itself, establish that every number in Northann's financial statements is false.

The numbers are now provisional

The FY2025 10-K reported $13.6 million of revenue, $3.58 million of gross profit and an $11.67 million net loss.

It also reported approximately $1.03 million of cash at year-end and $5.68 million of cash used in operating activities during the year.

Those figures show what investors were presented with in the disputed filing.

They should not, however, be treated as final financial reality.

Northann itself has said the FY2024 and FY2025 financial statements should not be relied upon pending re-audit.

So the numbers occupy an unusual position: they remain part of the documentary record, but the company has withdrawn reliance on them while the accounting work is redone.

Then there is the $11 million software question

The reporting problem becomes more consequential when viewed alongside Northann's capital structure.

In November 2025, Northann agreed to acquire proprietary supply-chain software and intellectual property from Kingsford Consultancy for $5 million, payable through 12.5 million Northann shares.

It separately agreed to pay $6 million in shares for software and intellectual property under a development agreement with Asia Resource Holdings.

Together, those transactions represented:

$11 million of stated consideration for 27.5 million shares.

At December 31, 2025, Northann reported 22.93 million common shares outstanding.

The subsequent issuance of 27.5 million shares was therefore approximately 120% of the company's year-end share count.

That calculation does not establish that either transaction was improper.

It shows why the accounting treatment and valuation of the transactions matter.

The software transactions were large relative to Northann's existing equity base. If the financial statements describing them need to be re-audited, the consequences extend beyond an accounting footnote. They can affect how investors understand the company's assets, equity and dilution.

The reporting problem became a market problem

The consequences did not remain inside Northann's financial statements.

Trading in Northann's securities was halted in June.

The company formed an Oversight Committee and retained outside counsel after the audit dispute emerged. Lin Li, who had held senior executive and board positions, subsequently left the company.

In August, Northann disclosed that NYSE American had commenced delisting proceedings, determining that the company was not suitable for continued listing under several provisions of the NYSE American Company Guide.

The company has requested an oral hearing to review that determination.

None of those events, by themselves, establishes fraud.

They show something narrower: a dispute over the integrity and completion of the company's financial reporting process developed into a broader governance, trading and listing problem.

A new auditor now has to rebuild the picture

On August 26, Northann's Audit Committee appointed TQ International, PLLC as its independent registered public accounting firm.

TQ is expected to audit the FY2025 financial statements and review interim financial information for March 31 and June 30, 2026.

That work now has two jobs.

The first is straightforward: determine what the company's financial statements should actually say.

The second is less straightforward and remains unanswered:

What happened to the audit opinion attributed to LAO that appeared in the original filing?

The documentary record currently establishes the contradiction.

Northann filed an annual report containing an audit opinion attributed to LAO.

LAO later said it had not prepared or authorized that opinion and had not completed the audit.

Northann subsequently told investors not to rely on the financial statements while a replacement auditor undertakes the work.

What the current record does not establish is who caused the disputed audit material to appear in the filing, whether anyone acted intentionally, or whether the underlying financial statements contain material accounting errors.

Those are separate questions, and they require separate evidence.

For now, the most important document may be the next audit itself.

Not because it will necessarily explain how the disputed opinion entered the filing, but because it should begin answering the more immediate question for investors:

What, if anything, in Northann's reported financial position can still be relied upon?
